doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Jazz education and the state of record sales
summary: He discusses jazz education booming as the music lost popularity, and why RIAA statistics undercount jazz sales by missing musicians' own CDs.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well we have just a couple of minutes left and I — recently there was a fellow who wrote in the Jazz Educators Network about the — he called it the “paradox of the jazz scene” and that jazz is now taught in almost every university and Jazz at Lincoln Center, and all the high schools and the whole thing, yet record sales are very small and even the musicians who play the music, the young people, don’t buy things that much anymore. Do you have any observations on the current state?

Well the whole phenomenon of jazz education is of course a very interesting one because as the music became less popular, less visible, jazz education boomed and there are hundreds of places where you can take courses in jazz. I think it’s very useful because most of the people that learn to play an instrument and learn to play jazz, one of the things that will stay with them and maybe for a lifetime is the fact that they can have the pleasure of playing for their own enjoyment with other people. Making a profession out of it is sometimes difficult. Yet there are people, for instance institutions like Berklee, have produced a lot of musicians who have become first class prominent professionals. But it’s something — it’s also I guess it has become a way for many — I wouldn’t say failed musicians, but musicians who have been unable for one reason or another to have profitable playing careers to become teachers. And many of them are very good, very able, and it’s provided also an income for really good players who couldn’t really make a good living playing anymore. But what you said about record sales, the industry promoted percentages have always been way off the mark because the record industry association, RIAA, is purely interested in major label products. They have never included anything from really small independent labels. They have never included jazz imports in their statistics. So when they say jazz sales only represents three percent that was always nonsense because all you had to do was — in the good old days — when there were record stores like Tower, if you walked into a Tower store why would they give so much space to jazz if it wasn’t selling more than three percent? That wouldn’t have made any sense at all. There were really miles and miles of jazz left there. So this was always very

questionable. But nowadays of course most jazz record sales are off statistics altogether because it’s musicians selling their CDs when they go out and perform. I mean that’s where you find most of what you see today. You go to a concert, at least that’s the case in New York, there’s a table there in front before you enter the hall there, there’s a table manned by a couple of people and there are stacks of CDs that represent the performer. And when you go out on the road, I know people who are friends of mine, they pack, they’ve got CDs in their car, you know, they’ve got boxes of CDs. That’s where the sales are. And they don’t enter the official statistics. It’s just like it’s said that CDs are vanishing. They’re not. I mean it’s true in the classical field too, the same thing happens there. So there is a lot of stuff still around but it’s off the beaten marketing path. And so I think people will continue to want to own a tangible item of something that they can play for their friends or whatever. You know all the other stuff that you can hear on your headphones and your earbuds, you know, it’s out in cyberspace. And I think there is a proprietary instinct in people. It’s the same thing with books. You know e-books and all that, it’s fine, but you still want to have — and also you want to be able to, you know your friends come to visit and they see all the books.
